title: Matching Pairs With Divisible Index Product
statement:
You get an array nums and a positive integer k. Count the index pairs (i, j) with 0 ≤ i < j < n where both of these hold:

  • nums[i] === nums[j], and
  • the product of the indexes, i · j, is divisible by k.

Indexes are 0-based, so any pair that uses index 0 has product 0, which every k divides.

examples.why: (0,2) and (0,4) have product 0, and (1,3) has product 3. The pair (2,4) has equal values but product 8, which 3 does not divide.
(0,1) and (0,2) pass because of index 0. (1,2) has product 2.
There are 6 equal pairs, but only the 5s at indexes 0, 2, 4 give products 0, 0 and 8. The 1s sit at odd indexes, with products 3, 5 and 15.

hints: With at most 100 values, checking every pair is perfectly fine. Write that first and get both conditions right.
Index 0 is special: its product with anything is 0, and 0 is divisible by every k.
To skip pairs that can never match, group indexes by value first and only compare indexes inside the same group.

explain.intuition:
Two conditions, both on the same pair, so the direct approach is to check every pair i < j: equal values, and (i * j) % k === 0. With n ≤ 100 that is under 5 000 checks, which is nothing.

A small refinement is to group indexes by value with a hash map, the way you would bucket list items by a key before diffing them. Pairs with different values are then never even looked at. That helps most when the values are spread out.
steps: For every i and every j > i: if nums[i] === nums[j] and (i * j) % k === 0, add one.
pitfalls: Using 1-based indexes. Then index 0 never shows up, and the pairs that use it are wrongly dropped or the products are all off.
Checking whether i % k === 0 or j % k === 0 alone. With k = 4, the pair (2, 6) has product 12, which passes even though neither index does.
Counting a pair twice by letting j start at 0 instead of i + 1.

solutions.title: Check every pair
solutions.idea: Two nested loops over i < j, testing both conditions.

solutions.title: Group indexes by value
solutions.idea: Bucket indexes by value in a hash map, then only test pairs inside one bucket.
solutions.time: O(n²) worst case, O(n + Σ group²) in general

followups: Now n is up to 100 000 and all values are equal. Count pairs whose index product is divisible by k faster than O(n²). (Hint: gcd(i, k).)
Count pairs whose index sum, instead of product, is divisible by k.
lcTitle: Count Equal and Divisible Pairs in an Array
